newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq, Jordan to sign oil pact Thurs, official says.
newsitem.headline: Iraq, Jordan to sign oil pact Thurs, official says.

text.p: Iraq and Jordan are expected to resolve their differences and sign on Thursday an oil agreement to supply the kingdom with its 1997 crude and refined products needs, a senior Jordanian official said.
"I hope that the oil agreement (between Iraq and Jordan) will be signed today (Thursday)," Jordan's Energy and Mineral Resources Hashem Dabbas told Reuters.
Dabbas, accompanied by Jordan's Trade and Industry Minister Ali Abu al-Ragheb and seniors Jordanian officials started on Thursday oil and trade talks in the Iraqi capital.
"Our talks with Iraq's oil and trade ministries will start today," al-Ragheb said.
Both Dabbas and Ragheb declined to comment on why Baghdad and Amman failed at the start of this month to conclude an accord under which Iraq would supply Jordan with its energy needs for 1997.

Jordanian officials have said Baghdad demanded higher prices for its oil exports -- around 75,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude and petroleum products. The amount is exempted from stringent U.N. embargoes banning Iraq from exporting its oil as punishment for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
After a meeting with Jordanian Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti in Amman earlier this week, Iraq's Deputy Premier Tareq Aziz said his country was committed to supplying Jordan with oil.

Since the 1991 Gulf War over Kuwait -- in which Amman sympathised with Baghdad -- Iraq exports 75,000 bpd to Jordan for which it paid market prices for 25,000 bpd and for another 25,000 bpd of products. The rest is at undisclosed concessionary terms.
The officials said Iraq had already agreed to Jordan's request to raise the oil supplies in 1997 by seven percent to meet growth in local consumption.

Jordanian businessmen also have their eyes set on an Iraqi oil-for-food deal signed with the United Nations. Under the pact -- its implementation started a month ago -- Baghdad is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil every six months to buy food and medicine for the Iraqi population.
They say they have won orders in tough competition to supply Iraq with a range of goods worth more than $120 million under the accord.
